Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Gameplay (4 players) 2.1 Phase 1: Setup 2.2 Phase 2: Shopping 2.3 Phase 3: Need Cards 2.4 Phase 4: Showing Off 2.4.1 Evaluating Needs 2.4.2 Scoring an Exhibition 2.5 Phase 5: Business 2.5.1 Selling Pets 2.5.2 Using Unused Imps 2.6 Phase 6: Aging 3 Final Scoring 4 Losing a Pet 5 Action Spaces 6 2/3 Player Variant 7 Double Symbol Variant 8 Forsight Variant Objective Run your pet shop, join exhibitions and sell pets to become the player with the highest reputation after 6 rounds. Gameplay (4 players) Phase 1: Setup All players get income. The starting player and the player on their left get 1 gold. The other two players get 2 gold. Add food in the food stands according to the exhibition tile. Put 2 new artifacts, 2 new cages, 1 addon and 3 new baby pets. If there are remaining size 2 pets, they grow up to size 3. If there are remaining size 3 pets, they are discarded and 1 meat is added. Reveal the next exhibition tiles and customers. Phase 2: Shopping All players simultaneously and secretly divide their imps and gold into groups. A group must have at least 1 imp, but can have any number of gold. You can have at most 6 groups. You don't need to assign all imps or all gold. When everyone is finished, reveal all groups. Send the groups starting with the largest size (imp+gold). If multiple players are tied, start with the starting player. If a group is sent, all gold with it goes to the bank. If you decide to keep it home, you take back the gold. Phase 3: Need Cards Place new cages and addons, which cannot be moved later, but can be removed or replaced. Put all pets in cages (1 pet in 1 cage), they can be moved later with any suffering and mutations on it. If you cannot put all pets in cages, you must release the remaining pets and lose reputation for it. Each player has 1 card of each colour in hand at any time except phase 3. Draw 1 card of the same color for each revealed color bar and assign one card for each matching colour bar. You can assign potions, which needs nothing, instead of a need card. Phase 4: Showing Off Evaluating Needs For each hunger need, spend a food token corresponding to the type of pet or put a suffering token on it. For each poop need, put a manure token in the cage. For each play need, hire an imp to entertain it or put a suffering token on it. An imp can play with two adjacent pets at once. If a pet’s anger needs exceed its cage’s strength, use one available imp for every anger need that is not handled by the cage or its addon, or it escapes and you lost it. All used imps for angry needs go to the hospital. If a pet’s magic needs exceed its cage’s antimagic, the pet mutates. Put 1 mutation token on the pet for each magic need that is not handled by the cage or its addon. If a pet has 2 or more mutations, it disappears and you lost it. If the total of manures and disease needs are larger than 2, put one suffering token on the pet for getting sick. Then place an additional suffering token for each point greater than 2. Discard need cards until you have 1 card of each colour, or 2-3 with related artifacts. If the number of suffering tokens on the pet is equal to or larger than its size, you lost it. Scoring an Exhibition Choose 1 of your pet to enter the exhibition or score your entire display. The symbols in the light frame count positively, while the symbols in the dark frame count negatively. If your exhibition score is 0 or less, you don't take part in the competition. The player with the highest score scores 8 reputation, then 6, 4 and 2. Phase 5: Business Selling Pets Starting from round 3, there are customers. They will buy 1 pet from each player if they like it. You can only sell pets that are at least size 4. [Rating: 1/10] Zooloretto with difficult to manage pets and hard to please customers. So perhaps it is closer to A Little Shop of Horrors. It becomes a difficult exercise of resource management, being blocked by your competitors and avoiding disasters.  Each turn is a puzzle to be solved. From the blind bidding for the turn order to the limited number of actions and resources, to matching your pets needs to the resources you have. This puzzle becomes more difficult as you acquire more pets. Not to mention the longer range problem of having the right kind of pet for the shows and customers.   It is a gamer's 

[Rating: 1/10] There's a good game in here somewhere, it's just hidden behind messy graphic design, fussy and over complex rules and bloated game length.  It's possible to be completely ruined by the luck of the draw with the 'needs' cards and realise you've lost with another 2 hours to play. If you draw the right cards you are guaranteed to win both the exhibition AND more points for selling your creature.   Not sure I'd ever want to play again but I'm also not completely ruling it out.  :star::nostar::nostar::nostar::nostar: Components :star::nostar::nostar::nostar::nostar: Artwork :star::star::nostar::nos

[Rating: 2/10] If a game is fun and interesting then I can excuse a rule book that is on par with MJ's Baseball career. Alas, Dungeon Petz seems to be some kind of huge practical joke to mock gamers. Thematically it's cringe worthy, and mechanically it's just tiresome. I will never play this again.

[Rating: 2/10] Played twice. Couldn't put the rule book down because trying to keep track of the action order each round was overwhelming. Decent game with interesting mechanisms, but in the end wasn't for us.

[Rating: 2/10] Two stars for the caterpillar and the other crazy animal paintings. But except for that, this game is not my taste: too complicated, too many pieces, too many rules, no thrill, no fun.

[Rating: 2/10] Overly complicated and too many competing mechanics. Poorly organized 20-page rulebook and the theme was way more tasteless than expected. You're basically running a puppy mill and there's more pet suffering and death than the cute box art and general synopsis would make you believe. Will never play again.

The player reference on the screens is effectively unusable because of how cluttered it is. The contents of the box are cheap. There’s no box insert for organization. The tokens are the cheapest on the market. The price point is way too high for the quality of the game. Okay, and that’s all before we get to the content. I probably owe the game anoher play but I'm not sure I'm inclined to keep playing it when there are better worker placement games out there.

[Rating: 2/10] Very rules-heavy, yet still felt fiddly most of the time. I also noticed some tonal inconsistencies between the theme and how mechanically heavy it is. It has some original parts that had potential but at the end it just isn’t worth the trouble or time to learn properly.
